## Supplementary sensitivity results (relative intakes)

The completed body-mass-relative sensitivity analyses did not overturn the primary analyses substantive conclusions. Mundlak, errors-in-variables, residual-correlation, and common-sample achieved and assignment-derived models remained broadly compatible with the primary curves and inferential pattern. The strict within-study curves were generally more attenuated in magnitude, indicating that part of the primary arm-level association may reflect between-study differences or non-random variation in achieved intake; critically, they did not reveal a large or clearly meaningful outcome gain from increasing intake that was hidden by the primary analysis. The similarity of the paired achieved- and assignment-derived analyses suggests that neither restriction to studies with reconstructible assignment nor the achieved-versus-prescribed exposure definition materially changed the broad conclusion. Models distinguishing protein addition from macronutrient substitution did not show a consistent advantage for either strategy across outcomes, RT conditions, and arm-level versus within-study estimands. Together, the sensitivities strengthen the robustness of the conclusion that large outcome gains from increasing intake, or losses from decreasing it, are not supported while reinforcing that, whilst the overall positive dose-response pattern is supported, the exact magnitude of the primary achieved-intake curve should not be interpreted as a causal per-protocol effect. See the [primary, Mundlak, and strict within-study comparison](https://jamessteeleii.github.io/protein_dose_response_meta/supplement/sensitivity-analyses.html#fig-core-relative-sensitivities), [arm-level sensitivity curves](https://jamessteeleii.github.io/protein_dose_response_meta/supplement/sensitivity-analyses.html#fig-relative-arm-curves), and [addition-versus-substitution results](https://jamessteeleii.github.io/protein_dose_response_meta/supplement/sensitivity-analyses.html#addition-versus-substitution-analyses).

## Direct muscle size or mass sensitivity results (relative intakes)

Restricting eligibility to the registered measurement methods (i.e., excluding regional trunk or skinfold derived outcomes) for the relative intake analyses produced dose-response estimates and inferential conclusions similar to those of the original measures of muscle size or mass-outcome analysis. The imaging/biopsy-only analysis also yielded similar intake contrasts with RT; without RT, the estimated association was steeper but substantially less precise. Neither restriction identified a supported contrast meeting the posterior-probability criterion for a meaningful outcome gain from increasing intake or loss from decreasing it. Local practical equivalence remained supported, although the equivalence regions were narrower in the imaging/biopsy-only analysis, particularly without RT. These comparisons reflect changes in both the measurements and the contributing studies, and therefore do not necessarily isolate measurement method as the cause of differences. The supplement shows the [dose–response curves for the three eligibility definitions](https://jamessteeleii.github.io/protein_dose_response_meta/supplement/muscle-measurement-sensitivity-analyses.html#fig-measurement-curves) and [local practical equivalence](https://jamessteeleii.github.io/protein_dose_response_meta/supplement/muscle-measurement-sensitivity-analyses.html#local-practical-equivalence).

## Absolute-intake and absolute-supplementation results

The exploratory primary analyses of absolute total protein intake and prescribed absolute supplemental protein dose broadly reproduced the pattern of the relative-intake analysis. Dose-response functions were generally modestly positive for whole-body lean/fat-free mass, measures of muscle mass or size, and strength, while function showed shallow curvature, and nearby absolute-dose contrasts were commonly supported as practically equivalent. No supported contrast attained the 95% posterior-probability criterion for a meaningful gain or loss for direct muscle mass or size, strength, or function. The exception was whole-body lean/fat-free mass within the RT category, where some very widely separated contrasts met the criterion for a meaningful difference. Low intakes of [51–67 g/day versus approximately 202–265 g/day or more of total intake](https://jamessteeleii.github.io/protein_dose_response_meta/supplement/absolute-intake-sensitivity-analyses.html#tbl-total-meaningful), and [0–7 g/day supplementation versus approximately 88–106 g/day](https://jamessteeleii.github.io/protein_dose_response_meta/supplement/absolute-supplementation-sensitivity-analyses.html#tbl-supplement-meaningful) yielded small but meaningful gains. However, these contrasts occurred in the sparsely represented exposure tails and none lay wholly within the central 90% exposure range. The supplements show the dose–response curves and supported contrasts for [absolute total intake](https://jamessteeleii.github.io/protein_dose_response_meta/supplement/absolute-intake-sensitivity-analyses.html#dose-response-results) and [absolute supplementation](https://jamessteeleii.github.io/protein_dose_response_meta/supplement/absolute-supplementation-sensitivity-analyses.html#dose-response-results).

## Age and duration interaction results (relative, absolute, and supplementation intakes)

Across the four outcomes and three protein-dose definitions, posterior mean differences in protein contrasts between the upper and lower age or duration quartile profiles were generally small within locally supported dose ranges. No locally supported comparison met the posterior-probability criterion for a difference exceeding 0.1 standardised units in either direction. Many differences met the practical-equivalence criterion, while others remained uncertain, particularly where empirical support was limited. See the [conditional predictions, paired contrasts, and profile support](https://jamessteeleii.github.io/protein_dose_response_meta/supplement/age-duration-interactions.html#doseresponse-results) and the [candidate counts and stacking weights](https://jamessteeleii.github.io/protein_dose_response_meta/supplement/age-duration-interactions.html#tbl-age-duration-weights).

## Training-status results (relative, absolute, and supplementation intakes)

Across the three protein-dose definitions, no supported trained-minus-untrained difference in a protein contrast reached the 95% posterior-probability criterion for meaningful moderation of whole-body lean/fat-free mass, measures of muscle size or mass, or strength. Many differences met the practical-equivalence criterion. Uncertainty remained, particularly for strength in the relative- and absolute-total-intake analyses. Physical-function comparisons were descriptive because only one or two trained studies contributed per dose definition and no comparison met the support criterion. The supplement shows the [dose–response curves and paired contrasts](https://jamessteeleii.github.io/protein_dose_response_meta/supplement/training-status.html#doseresponse-results) and [study counts and dose support](https://jamessteeleii.github.io/protein_dose_response_meta/supplement/training-status.html#tbl-training-status-support).

# Discussion

To our knowledge this is the largest systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials conducted to date exploring the association of protein intake with changes in whole body lean/fat free mass, measures of muscle size or mass, strength, and physical function in healthy adults. Across all outcomes, whilst dose-response functions were typically modestly positive, particularly with RT, neither increasing nor decreasing intake within the observed range met the criterion for a meaningful change in outcome whether a gain from increasing intake or a loss from decreasing it. Thus, despite directional dose-response associations, it is far less clear that differences in protein intakes across the ranges examined in the included studies are associated with meaningful differences in outcomes. Instead, there is clearer evidence for local practical equivalence between protein intakes.

The local equivalence between protein intakes does not imply that protein intake has no impact upon the outcomes examined, but that changes within these local regions are likely to yield outcomes that are practically equivalent, at least according to our registered SESOI. Across all outcomes our results suggest that, from a current protein intake within the ranges examined, increases or decreases of approximately 0.2 to 0.5 g/kg/day do not result in meaningfully different outcomes. This one-sided distance is distinct from the full lower-to-upper equivalence-window width of approximately 0.4 to 0.9 g/kg/day. Outside these local ranges, neither increases nor decreases in intake met our pre-registered SESOI for a meaningful outcome change; instead, estimates for more widely separated intakes were far less certain, reflecting the lack of current data for such comparisons.

We examined a range of candidate dose-response models in our analysis and utilised a Bayesian model-averaging approach [@hinneConceptualIntroductionBayesian2020] in order to incorporate uncertainty about the function form which might best describe the data. Previous modelling of dose-response functions has often implicitly included sharp "breakpoints" in the analyses (~1.2 to 1.6 g/kg/day) either through categorical treatment of intakes [@nunesSystematicReviewMetaanalysis2022], estimation of single breakpoints from piecewise models [@mortonSystematicReviewMetaanalysis2018], or using fixed inflexion points in non-linear modelling [@tagawaDoseResponseRelationship2021; @tagawaSynergisticEffectIncreased2022]. In contrast, our model-averaged dose response function did not identify a sharp optimal intake coincident with a "breakpoint" implying any kind of plateau in the association between protein intake and outcomes. This was despite including some candidate models with a function form implying a precise "breakpoint" (i.e., the linear-spline models with a knot at 1.6 g/kg/day). The distributed model weights (see [final stacking weights](https://jamessteeleii.github.io/protein_dose_response_meta/supplement/preregistration-deviations.html#tbl-stacking-weights)) instead demonstrate genuine function form uncertainty in the underlying data generating process meaning no single dose response shape should be treated as established. The overall model averaged dose-response function then should be treated as a candidate to take forward for further severe testing of its implied contrasts, and the implied magnitude of these could be used in ensuring that sufficiently powered/precise RCT designs are used for these tests.

We examined several plausible moderators of the protein intake dose-response including participation in RT, age, study duration, and training status. Studies show that RT increases muscle protein turnover and enhances the protein-synthetic response to amino acid provision, providing a plausible basis for an interaction between protein availability and the exercise stimulus [@bioloAbundantSupplyAmino1997; @phillipsMixedMuscleProtein1997], whereas in the absence of an RT stimulus muscle protein synthesis saturates at modest protein doses and additional amino acids are largely directed to oxidation rather than accretion [@mooreIngestedProteinDose2009; @witardMyofibrillarMuscleProtein2014]. Similarly older adults require a larger relative protein dose in a single meal to maximise muscle protein synthesis than younger adults [@mooreProteinIngestionStimulate2015]. Further, during RT, early increases in muscle protein synthesis partly reflect repair following unaccustomed exercise; as muscle damage subsides, synthesis becomes more closely associated with hypertrophy [@damasResistanceTrainingInduced2016]. But, the effects of RT itself tend to diminish over duration of exposure [@steeleLongTermTimeCourseStrength2023; @robertsModelingTrajectorySkeletal2026] resulting in strongly attenuated effects in well trained participants [@gschneidnerEffectsLengthenedpartialRange2025; @steeleTestHigherLower2026]. This provides a physiological reason to consider both exposure duration and prior training experience as both may affect not only RTs effects but plausibly the effects of protein too. However, despite their plausibility, comparison of dose-response functions between conditions with participation of RT compared to no RT, across ages, study durations, and both untrained and trained participants, we found little moderating effects across outcomes. The exception was for whole body lean/fat free mass and RT where there was a somewhat clearer tendency for modest association between higher protein intakes and outcomes when participating in RT as compared to a flatter function without. However, given participation in RT is a principally more effective adaptive stimulus for this outcome the overall modest effects of protein intake in comparison retain biological plausibility. When not participating in RT protein intake may have even less influence when habitual intake is already adequate consistent with adaptive metabolic demand and protein-stat accounts of regulation [@millwardDietaryProteinMuscle2025]. Yet, the present evidence does not clearly establish that protein intake dose-response associations across outcomes differ meaningfully when participating, or not, in RT. Additionally, in exploratory model-averaged analyses restricted to RT studies, we also found little moderating effect of study-reported training status comparing trained and untrained groups[^training-status-physical-function]. This held for relative protein intake, absolute total intake, and absolute supplementation. Many supported differences met the criterion for practical equivalence, while others remained uncertain, particularly for strength in the relative and absolute total intake analyses.

[^training-status-physical-function]: Physical-function estimates were descriptive because [too few studies included trained participants](https://jamessteeleii.github.io/protein_dose_response_meta/supplement/training-status.html#tbl-training-status-support) to support the comparison.

Despite the generally trivial effects of differing protein intakes and the lack of moderating effects by participation in RT, age, study duration, and training status in our results, the uncertainty in aspects of our findings is particularly relevant to well-trained participants and competitive athletes who may be seeking to optimise outcomes. Short trials, limited sample sizes, and sparse evidence jointly covering trained participants, direct contrasts between low and high intakes, and lack of long follow-up periods leave the question of whether a worthwhile benefit from higher intakes over longer periods remains possible for experienced participants in strength and aesthetic sports, including bodybuilding, despite trivial average effects. Further, individuals in such populations may hold different personal SESOIs in comparison to our pre-registered SESOI used here and so may still reasonably interpret the trivial average effects reported as meaningful to them and their context. But, it should be noted that even with smaller SESOIs most contrasts would remain uncertain for the kinds of contrasts described i.e., low versus high intakes in trained populations participating in RT. Evidence remains sparse for contrasts implied by these areas of the dose-response curves presented and so future research should perhaps be directed at these but be aware that the typical sample sizes in the present body of literature are woefully inadequate with respect to power/precision to detect the magnitudes of average effects estimated in our present results[^trial-power]. Further, these populations typically also seek to maximise muscle gain while reducing fat mass, and therefore undertake periods of energy deficit. We excluded interventions intended to induce weight loss and did not model energy balance directly as a moderator, so the present findings do not resolve protein dose responses during deliberate energy restriction. Short-term energy deficit can suppress resting muscle protein synthesis [@aretaReducedRestingSkeletal2014]. Previous syntheses addressing this context suggest that intakes above the RDA can attenuate lean-mass loss during energy restriction [@hudsonProteinIntakeGreater2020], and that higher intakes are associated with more favourable fat-free-mass changes in energy-restricted, resistance-trained participants, although the latter findings remain exploratory [@refaloEffectDietaryProtein2026]. Preserving fat-free mass during a deficit is also a distinct objective from maximising muscle gain. Neither those findings nor our results establish an optimal intake for athletes pursuing both goals, and our local equivalence findings should not be assumed to generalise to that setting. Again, this is a further area that future research should target.

[^trial-power]: To illustrate we can consider the power and sample sizes implied by the model-based estimates from our results. For each dose comparison, we used the smallest absolute posterior mean contrast across whole-body lean/fat-free mass, measures of muscle size or mass, and strength in the primary RT analyses appraised with GRADE (age 25 years, 12 weeks). We used pooled RT estimates because the lowest observed intake in trained RT samples was 0.87 g/kg/day. For 0.8 versus 1.6, 0.8 versus 2.4, and 1.6 versus 2.4 g/kg/day, the selected effects were 0.0695, 0.1598, and 0.0569 baseline SDs, respectively. The first two were for whole-body lean/fat-free mass and the third was for strength. If these were the true between-arm differences in mean change, a two-sided two-sample *t*-test at $\alpha = 0.05$ with equal allocation, equal baseline and follow-up SDs, and a baseline to follow-up correlation of 0.80 would have conditional power of 5.7%, 8.7%, and 5.5% at 11 participants per arm (trained RT median), and 5.9%, 9.9%, and 5.6% at 14 per arm (all RT median), respectively. Achieving 80% power would require 1,302, 247, and 1,942 analysable participants per arm, respectively. Other means of increasing power such as higher frequency measurement and handling of covariance structures, or use of baseline prognostic covariates may help to improve this. But, given the extremely low power in the typical trial, and the enormous sample sizes required to achieve reasonable power, these will only help things so much.

The sensitivity analyses, across all protein exposure definitions, clarify the causal interpretation of the primary dose-response results. The Mundlak and strict within-study models moved identification towards randomised comparisons within trials, and the latter were generally more attenuated in magnitude than the primary arm-level associations. This suggests that the magnitude of the primary dose-response results may include at least some between-study differences or post-randomisation components and may in fact overstate the magnitude of the causal effect of changing intake. Conversely, the paired achieved- and assignment-derived analyses were broadly similar, and explicitly modelling intake measurement error or residual within-study correlation did not reveal any substantively different association. The addition-versus-substitution protein intake strategy analyses, examined to determine if energy adjustment (i.e., protein intake either increased energy intake or protein intake substituted other macronutrients) was conducted to see if the dose response associations differed when these different estimands were considered [@ortegaMetaanalysesDietaryExposures2026]. However, it also did not identify a consistent strategy advantage. There was also little impact of measurement approaches for muscle size or mass with similar dose-response curves with the inclusion of regionally derived outcomes from DXA, BIA, or skinfolds and sensitivity analyses including only direct MRI, CT, US, and biopsy muscle measurements. The broad small-effect conclusion is therefore robust across complementary assumptions. The primary absolute-intake and absolute supplementation dose analyses did not materially alter the overall interpretation based on relative intake. They provide a limited indication that extremely widely separated absolute doses may be associated with a meaningful difference in whole-body lean/fat-free mass during RT, but this was limited to contrasts with sparse high-dose observations and was not reproduced across the other outcomes. The risk-of-bias, publication-bias, and GRADE findings further qualify the strength of our conclusions. Most trials raised some concerns or were at high risk of bias for their index result, publication-bias-adjusted estimates were appreciably attenuated, and certainty was low or very low for every assessed dose contrast. The failure to establish a meaningful outcome gain from increasing intake, or loss from decreasing it, should therefore not be interpreted as precise evidence that all more widely separated intakes are equivalent. Rather, the clearest positive inference is local practical equivalence, while estimates for larger contrasts remain uncertain and the overall evidence base warrants caution.

This review both inherits strengths from the previous review of Nunes et al. [-@nunesSystematicReviewMetaanalysis2022] and adds several new strengths in comparison with that and other previous evidence syntheses. The evidence base was expanded to include studies published since the previous review, and data extraction and modelling were expanded to include more data than previously used from the included studies; compared with the previous review, the updated dataset contained approximately five times as many whole-body lean/fat free mass or measures of muscle size or mass contrasts, over four times as many strength contrasts, and nearly six times as many function contrasts. We also directly incorporated uncertainty about dose-response functional form through model averaging and provide cautious interpretations based on our preregistered SESOI. Lastly, although some deviations were required to address model-fitting diagnostic issues in the final dataset, all are thoroughly and transparently reported.

There are, however, still limitations to this review and the broader body of evidence regarding the effects of protein intake. As already noted, data remain sparse at the extremes of intake, both below the RDA and very high intakes, and thus it is difficult to draw certain inferences regarding comparatively high or low protein intakes. Most included studies examined relatively short intervention durations, typically 10-12 weeks. Although the exploratory duration analyses did not identify meaningful moderation within locally supported ranges, they do not establish whether protein contrasts become smaller or larger over substantially longer exposure, either with or without participation in RT. The heterogeneity of outcome operationalisations, whilst all *a priori* deemed valid for the constructs of interest, required standardisation of contrasts and thereby limits practical interpretation; however, as noted in the methods, we included reference values to aid interpretation of the standardised mean changes and their magnitudes are not drastically different than what might have been expected given the typical magnitude of effects for RT alone [@steeleMetaanalysisVariationSport2023]. Considering these reference values, full lower-to-upper local practical-equivalence windows of approximately 0.4 to 0.9 g/kg/day amount to contrasts of roughly $\lessapprox0.5$ kg whole-body lean/fat-free mass mass, $\lessapprox0.05$ cm of muscle thickness, and $\lessapprox5$ kg for one-repetition maximum. Outcome covariances were not reported within studies and were therefore treated as independent. A proportion of eligible contrasts also had to be excluded, most commonly because protein intake or sufficient outcome data were unavailable, so resulting selection bias cannot be ruled out. Characteristics such as age, training status, sex, energy balance, clinical conditions such as frailty, protein quality and distribution, and RT programme design may modify responses but cannot all be resolved reliably from study-level synthesis. Lastly, though only indicative, our results suggest high risk of bias, including possible publication bias or other selection bias effects, in this trial literature and as such even our strongest conclusions retain at best a low level of certainty following GRADE.

Future trials provide severe tests of the implied dose-response functions and contrasts from our model-averaged results while addressing limitations of the present literature including risks of bias. Pre-registered studies of longer interventions, with larger samples, repeated dietary measurements, adherence assessment, and standardised RT prescriptions, together with better reporting of baseline, follow-up, and change-score variability, within-participant correlations, and outcome covariances, would strengthen subsequent synthesis. Open data would enable some missing quantities to be recovered and facilitate individual-participant-data analyses of potential effect modification by baseline intake, age, training experience, sex, body composition, and energy status. Most studies randomise participants to additional absolute supplementation or a prescribed intake target, for which intention-to-treat effects can be estimated, whereas achieved intake is post-randomisation and may be confounded by determinants of adherence and diet. Trials intended to estimate per-protocol effects of sustained intake should therefore collect the longitudinal intake, adherence, prognostic, and co-intervention information needed for appropriate adjustment. Future studies should also target the more uncertain contrasts implied by the model-averaged functions, especially comparisons between lower and higher intakes across the empirically supported ranges. They should also consider approaches to help achieve the relatively large sample sizes or required for their detection when testing against a point zero null (e.g., multi-site randomised trials) or improve power through other means (e.g., pre-registered prognostic covariates or higher frequency outcome measurement and covariance handling), or consider determining *a priori* a justifiable SESOI for which to test equivalence against if the effect magnitudes estimated by our models are deemed to be to small to be practically meaningful for a given population and context.

# Conclusion
The results of this updated systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis suggest that, within the protein-intake ranges represented in the available trials, the evidence most clearly supports local practical equivalence than a meaningful change in outcome from moving intake in either direction i.e., increasing or decreasing intake. The model-averaged functions showed a modest positive association between protein intake and the examined outcomes and so those wishing to maximise outcomes may see it as reasonable to aim for higher protein intakes. However, the estimates were not sufficiently precise to establish that the gain from increasing intake, or the loss from decreasing it, exceeded our *a priori* determined practically meaningful threshold. From a given current intake, directional changes of approximately 0.2 to 0.5 g/kg/day were generally supported as practically equivalent; expressed as the full lower-to-upper window, this corresponds to approximately 0.4 to 0.9 g/kg/day. More distant comparisons were generally uncertain rather than demonstrably meaningful or equivalent. The sensitivity analyses supported this broad conclusion but indicated that the primary achieved-intake curves should not be interpreted as fully causal and may slightly overestimate the magnitude of causal effects. Together with some or high risk of bias, attenuation after publication-bias adjustment, and low or very low GRADE certainty, these findings suggest that the effects of varied protein intakes are at best small and do not identify a sharp "breakpoint" indicating an optimum intake. Comparisons between more widely separated intakes, and the extent to which the observed associations represent causal dose effects, remain uncertain. As such, we suggest that practical recommendations for intakes should based upon other considerations than their effectiveness for the outcomes examined here and that future research should make concerted attempts to address the shortcomings of the current body of literature.
